content: 1. The 2008 study in Logy and Nutrition discusses the implications of infant and young child feeding practices on health outcomes, emphasizing the importance of proper nutrition during early childhood. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF recommend exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life, followed by the introduction of complementary foods while continuing breastfeeding for up to two years or beyond. 3. WHO provides detailed guidelines on complementary feeding practices for breastfed children, emphasizing the timing, quality, and safety of introduced foods. 4. UNICEF's 2011 Programming Guide outlines strategies for improving infant and young child feeding (IYCF) practices globally, focusing on nutrition and health outcomes. 5. Victora et al. (2016) in The Lancet explore the epidemiology, mechanisms, and lifelong effects of breastfeeding, highlighting its critical role in reducing mortality and improving health outcomes. 6. Rollins et al. (2016) in The Lancet discuss the economic and health benefits of investing in breastfeeding promotion and the necessary steps to improve breastfeeding practices worldwide. 7. WHO's 2003 guiding principles for complementary feeding emphasize the importance of timely introduction of nutrient-rich foods to support optimal growth and development in breastfed children. 8. WHO's fact sheet on malnutrition highlights the global burden of undernutrition and its impact on child health and development. 9. UNICEF's 2019 report, The State of the World’s Children, examines the challenges of child nutrition in a changing world, focusing on the importance of healthy diets for growth and development. 10. Theurich et al. (2020) in Nutrition Reviews analyze the long-term health implications of complementary feeding practices, emphasizing the need for evidence-based guidelines. 11. Przyrembel (2012) in Annals of Nutrition and Metabolism discusses the timing of complementary food introduction and its shortand long-term health consequences. 12. UNICEF's 2021 IYCF data provides insights into global feeding practices and their impact on child health and nutrition. 13. Carletti et al. (2017) in Nutrients investigate parental compliance with WHO recommendations on complementary feeding in a cohort of infants in Northeast Italy. 14. McAndrew et al. (2012) in the Infant Feeding Survey provide data on feeding practices in the UK, highlighting trends and challenges in infant nutrition. 15. Duong et al. (2005) in Acta Paediatrica examine the introduction of complementary foods within the first six months postpartum in rural Vietnam, identifying associated factors and outcomes. 16. Inoue and Binns (2014) in Nutrients review the introduction of solid foods to infants in the Asia-Pacific region, discussing cultural and nutritional considerations. 17. Wang et al. (2019) in BMC Public Health identify factors associated with early complementary feeding and the consumption of non-recommended foods among Dutch infants. 18. Agostoni and Przyrembel (2013) in Evidence-Based Research in Pediatric Nutrition explore the timing of complementary food introduction and its impact on later health outcomes. 19. Kramer and Kakuma (2012) in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews evaluate the optimal duration of exclusive breastfeeding and its health benefits. 20. Qasem et al. (2015) in BMC Pediatrics conduct a systematic review on the age of first complementary feeding and its implications for infant health. 21. Hannan et al. (2009) in Biological Trace Element Research examine maternal milk concentrations of zinc, iron, selenium, and iodine and their relationship to dietary intakes. 22. Michaelsen et al. (1994) in Acta Paediatrica study zinc intake, status, and growth in a longitudinal study of healthy Danish infants. 23. Pearce et al. (2013) in the International Journal of Obesity review the timing of complementary feeding and its association with childhood obesity risk. 24. Seach et al. (2010) in the International Journal of Obesity find that delayed introduction of solid foods reduces the risk of child overweight and obesity at 10 years of age. 25. Fall et al. (2011) in the International Journal of Epidemiology analyze infant feeding patterns and cardiovascular risk factors in young adulthood across five lowand middle-income countries. 26. Garden et al. (2012) in Nutrients explore the relationship between early life food intake and health outcomes at five years of age. 27. Lin et al. (2013) in Pediatrics investigate the timing of solid food introduction and its association with obesity in Hong Kong’s Children of 1997 birth cohort. 28. Neutzling et al. (2009) in the International Journal of Pediatric Obesity study the relationship between infant feeding and obesity at 11 years in a prospective birth cohort. 29. Symon et al. (2017) in the Singapore Medical Journal examine whether early introduction of solids promotes obesity. 30. Matos et al. (2014) in Cadernos de Saúde Pública analyze dietary patterns of children under five in Bahia State, Brazil, and their implications for health. 31. Weng et al. (2012) in Archives of Disease in Childhood conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis of risk factors for childhood overweight identifiable during infancy. 32. Clayton et al. (2013) in Pediatrics investigate the prevalence and reasons for early introduction of solid foods, with variations by milk feeding type. 33. The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2020) summarize existing guidance on feeding infants and children from birth to 24 months. 34. Fewtrell et al. (2017) in the Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition present a position paper on complementary feeding by the European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Nutrition. 35. Huh et al. (2011) in Pediatrics examine the timing of solid food introduction and its risk of obesity in preschool-aged children. 36. Moss and Yeaton (2014) in the Maternal and Child Health Journal highlight the protective benefits of breastfeeding and delaying solid foods for early childhood weight status. 37. Daniels et al. (2015) in the Australian and New Zealand Journal of Public Health review evidence on the timing of solid introduction in an obesogenic environment. 38. Covidence systematic review software facilitates evidence synthesis for health research. 39. Higgins et al. (2016) in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews introduce a revised tool for assessing bias in randomized trials. 40. WHO's fact sheet on falls addresses the global burden and prevention strategies. 41. The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (2019) provides a quality assessment tool for observational cohort and cross-sectional studies. 42. Iannotti et al. (2017) in Pediatrics evaluate the impact of eggs in early complementary feeding on child growth in a randomized controlled trial. 43. Stewart et al. (2017) in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition assess the effect of eggs on early child growth in rural Malawi. 44. The EFSA Panel on Nutrition (2019) in the EFSA Journal determines the appropriate age range for introducing complementary feeding into an infant's diet. 45. Birbilis et al. (2013) in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition link adolescent obesity to perinatal risk factors, parental BMI, and sociodemographic characteristics. 46. De Beer et al. (2015) in the International Journal of Obesity study associations between infant feeding, linear growth, and weight gain during early life with childhood body composition. 47. Elalfy et al. (2012) in Nutrition Research identify milk feeding patterns and family size as risk factors for iron deficiency anemia among poor Egyptian infants. 48. Gebreweld et al. (2019) in PLOS One report the prevalence of anemia and associated factors among children under five in Northeast Ethiopia. 49. Sreedhara and Banapurmath (2014) in Current Pediatric Research examine the nutritional status of infants in relation to complementary feeding practices. 50. Vafa et al. (2012) in the Journal of Health, Population, and Nutrition explore the relationship between breastfeeding and childhood obesity. 51. Zheng et al. (2015) in the Journal of Pediatrics study complementary feeding and childhood adiposity in a large Chinese cohort. 52. Abraham et al. (2012) in Public Health Nutrition analyze infant feeding in relation to eating patterns in the second year of life and weight status in the fourth year. 53. Caleyachetty et al. (2013) in Maternal and Child Nutrition investigate breastfeeding duration, age of starting solids, and high BMI risk in Indian children. 54. Gooze et al. (2011) in The Journal of Pediatrics study the relationship between feeding practices and obesity in US children at five years of age. 55. Morgan et al. (2004) in Archives of Disease in Childhood examine the influence of weaning on growth and health up to 18 months. 56. Quigley et al. (2009) in Archives of Disease in Childhood investigate infant feeding, solid foods, and hospitalization in the first eight months after birth. 57. Van Rossum et al. (2013) in the British Journal of Nutrition analyze weight change before and after the introduction of solids in a longitudinal birth cohort. 58. Wolman (1984) in the Journal of the American Dietetic Association examines feeding practices in infancy and the prevalence of obesity in preschool children. 59. Zutavern et al. (2004) in Archives of Disease in Childhood study the introduction of solids in relation to asthma and eczema. 60. Fergusson et al. (1983) in Archives of Disease in Childhood explore the relationship between infant diet and asthma. 61. Nagahori et al. (2017) in the Journal of General and Family Medicine report malnutrition among vaccinated children aged 0-5 years in Cameroon. 62. Wright et al. (2004) in Archives of Disease in Childhood investigate reasons for early weaning in a prospective population-based cohort study. 63. Azad et al. (2018) in Pediatrics separate the effects of breast milk, breastfeeding, and formula feeding on infant weight gain. 64. Briaux et al. (2019) in Maternal and Child Nutrition examine age-related differences in complementary feeding practices and child growth in rural Togo. 65. Ekelund et al. (2021) in the International Breastfeeding Journal study the duration of breastfeeding, age at complementary food introduction, and allergy-related diseases. 66. Lee et al. (2020) in Clinical and Experimental Pediatrics investigate the influence of complementary food introduction on asthma and atopic dermatitis in Korean children. 67. Lossius et al. (2018) in The Journal of Pediatrics study breastfeeding and the risk of childhood asthma in a prospective cohort. 68. Ogbo et al. (2018) in Tropical Medicine and Health analyze the association between infant feeding practices and diarrhea in Tanzanian children. 69. Kim et al. (2011) in Pediatric Allergy and Immunology report the incidence and risk factors of immediate-type food allergy during the first year of life in Korean infants. 70. Luccioli et al. (2014) in Pediatrics examine infant feeding practices and reported food allergies at six years of age. 71. Forsyth et al. (1993) in BMJ study the relationship between early solid food introduction and weight and illnesses during the first two years of life. 72. Cohen et al. (1994) in The Lancet investigate the effects of complementary food introduction on breast milk intake, total energy intake, and growth in Honduran infants. 73. Dewey et al. (2004) in the Journal of Nutrition find that exclusive breastfeeding for six months with iron supplementation maintains adequate micronutrient status in low-birth-weight infants. 74. Gupta et al. (2017) in The Lancet Global Health compare complementary feeding at four versus six months of age for preterm infants in a randomized trial. 75. Marriott et al. (2003) in Archives of Disease in Childhood study weaning practices in preterm infants in a randomized controlled trial. 76. Brion et al. (2020) in the Journal of Perinatology examine the association of complementary food initiation and type with BMI and weight-for-length at 12 months in preterm infants. 77. Supadmi et al. (2020) in the Pakistan Journal of Nutrition analyze exclusive breastfeeding, complementary food, and nutritional status in premature infants in Indonesia. 78. Brown et al. (1989) in Pediatrics study infant feeding practices and their relationship with diarrheal and other diseases in Lima, Peru. 79. Khadivzadeh and Parsai (2014) examine the effects of exclusive breastfeeding and complementary feeding on infant growth.
